sec.p: In the case where Δs=Δt\begin{document}$\Delta s=\Delta t$\end{document}, the rate parameter in Equation 9 will lead to biased estimates for the decay rate; if surveys are consistently conducted soon after a mass campaign, the empirical age distribution will be biased towards younger nets, such that the fitted rate parameter for the distribution in Equation 9 would overestimate the true decay rate; the converse would hold true when surveys are consistently conducted immediately prior to a mass campaign. Given the frequency of DHS surveys can vary significantly between countries, for countries with fewer surveys, there is an increased risk this may lead to biased estimates in decay rates. For example, if surveys are systematically conducted immediately after a mass distribution campaign, this will lead to overestimates in the decay rates. Therefore, to attempt to reduce this risk of bias, we use a hierarchical model to pool information over larger spatial scales with the following positive-truncated normal (N>0\begin{document}$\text{N}_{ \gt 0}$\end{document}) prior distributions:

sec.title: Continent-level hyperhyperpriors:
sec.p: Under our hierarchical model, there is a country-level random effect on the region-specific mean ITN retention time (γi−1\begin{document}$\gamma_{i}^{-1}$\end{document}, Equation 11). There is then a continent-level random effect on the country-specific mean ITN retention time (γζ(i)−1\begin{document}$\gamma_{\zeta(i)}^{-1}$\end{document}, Equation 12), where ζ(i)\begin{document}$\zeta(i)$\end{document} is the country of region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}. Standard deviations are modelled in an analogous manner using a hierarchical structure (Equation 13).

We then used a weakly informative hyperhyperprior for the continent-wide mean retention time estimate (γ0−1\begin{document}$\gamma_{0}^{-1}$\end{document}, Equation 14), with a mean and standard deviation of 24 and 12 months, respectively. A prior mean of 24 months broadly reflects findings from previous studies (Bhatt et al., 2015; Bertozzi-Villa et al., 2021), yet Equation 14 cautiously imposes a prior belief there is a 95% probability the continent-wide mean is between 3.9 and 47.6 months.

The between-country standard deviation in mean ITN retention time (σ0\begin{document}$\sigma_{0}$\end{document}, Equation 15) is then assumed a priori to have a mean and standard deviation of 1 month. Since the central 95% range of a N>0(1,1)\begin{document}$\text{N}_{ \gt 0}\left(1,1\right)$\end{document} distribution is [0.08, 3.03], conditional on values of σ0\begin{document}$\sigma_{0}$\end{document} near the upper tail of this prior would allow roughly 95% of country-level means to lie within approximately 6 months of the continental mean a priori. This is broadly in line with previous estimates by Bhatt et al., 2015 who estimated 85% (n=40) of sub-Saharan African countries had a median retention time between 1.5 and 2.5 years; the smooth-compact loss function assumed in that study leads to similar mean and median estimates. Imposing a marginally tighter inter-country variance than previous studies is nevertheless intentional. This is because the derivation that the age distribution of ITNs when pooled across surveys tends to the same distribution as the duration of continuous access assumes periodic distribution of ITNs is long-standing and that a sufficiently large number of surveys have been conducted without inherent bias in their timings relative to mass campaigns. While mass campaigns have been conducted for roughly an order of magnitude greater than expected ITN retention times, in countries where more Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS), which are often conducted 6 months after a campaign, than other DHS surveys that are not timed in relation to campaigns, this may create an inherent bias that overestimates the decay rate of ITN use (and access). Assuming a random effect a priori with a slightly smaller variance than indicated in previous studies helps to mitigate bias arising from survey timings for data-sparse countries.

The mean (χ0\begin{document}$\chi_{0}$\end{document}, Equation 16) and standard deviation (ω0\begin{document}$\omega_{0}$\end{document}, Equation 17) of the inter-regional standard deviation of mean ITN retention times within each country (σζ\begin{document}$\sigma_{\zeta}$\end{document}) are also assumed a priori to have means and standard deviations of 1 month. Here χ0\begin{document}$\chi_{0}$\end{document} and ω0\begin{document}$\omega_{0}$\end{document}, respectively, govern the magnitude and variability of within-country heterogeneity in mean ITN retention times. Given the upper bound of the 95% range of these hyperhyperprior distributions is approximately 3 months, this would correspond to inter-regional standard deviations up to approximately 9 months in extreme cases where σζ\begin{document}$\sigma_{\zeta}$\end{document} has values around χ0+2ω0\begin{document}$\chi_{0}+2\omega_{0}$\end{document}. Conditional on such values, 95% of regional mean retention times would lie within approximately ±2σζ≈±18\begin{document}$\pm 2\sigma_{\zeta}\approx\pm 18$\end{document} months of the country mean. Although the hyperhyperpriors (which govern inter-regional variability) assumed in Equations 16 and 17 are the same as the hyperprior (which governs between-country variability) assumed in Equation (15), the model structure assumes random effects of greater magnitude between regions than between countries. As discussed, we have assumed a marginally narrower prior belief in inter-country variability than findings from previous studies (Bhatt et al., 2015; Bertozzi-Villa et al., 2021) to minimise the risk of survey timing biasing our estimates. Since DHS surveys and mass campaigns are often conducted at similar timings within a country, these biases are likely to be conserved across regions, allowing for greater scope to assume greater inter-regional variability a priori.

Under our assumption that nets are discarded at a constant rate within each subnational region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}, the age, αil\begin{document}$\alpha_{il}$\end{document}, of each net l\begin{document}$l$\end{document} is modelled as exponentially distributed with rate γi\begin{document}$\gamma_{i}$\end{document}. However, as DHS surveys do not record ages of nets greater than 36 months, but report them as being older than this threshold, we therefore treat these observations as right-censored at 36.5 months (due to whole-month rounding), giving a likelihood:(18)π(αil∣γi)={f(αil;γi), ifαil≤361−F(36.5;γi), otherwise\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \pi \left(\alpha_{il}\mid \gamma_{i} \right) = \begin{cases} f \left(\alpha_{il}; \gamma_{i} \right)&\text{, if}\, \alpha_{il}\leq 36 \\ 1 - F \left(36.5; \gamma_{i} \right)&\text{, otherwise}\end{cases} $$\end{document}
where f(α;γ)\begin{document}$f(\alpha;\gamma)$\end{document} and F(α;γ)\begin{document}$F(\alpha;\gamma)$\end{document} are Exponential density and cumulative distribution functions, respectively.

To correct for non-random probabilities of households being sampled in DHS surveys, we also conduct the fitting process using pseudo-counts, Mir\begin{document}$M_{ir}$\end{document}, of the number of nets of a given age α=r\begin{document}$\alpha=r$\end{document} in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}, where:(19)Mir=[∑l=1Nirwil]\begin{document}$$\displaystyle M_{ir}= \left[\sum_{l=1}^{N_{ir}}w_{il}\right] $$\end{document}

given Nir\begin{document}$N_{ir}$\end{document} is the surveyed number of nets of age r\begin{document}$r$\end{document} in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}, wil\begin{document}$w_{il}$\end{document} is the household survey weight for net l\begin{document}$l$\end{document}, while [·] denotes a standard rounding function. As DHS surveys have a stratified sampling design each household has a unique probability of being sampled within each region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}. To account for these non-random probabilities of households being surveyed, each net l\begin{document}$l$\end{document} that is recorded has an associated household weighting, wil\begin{document}$w_{il}$\end{document}. The DHS also scales these weightings by a factor of 106; our notation here of wil\begin{document}$w_{il}$\end{document} corrects for this scaling, and is therefore equal to the reported DHS household weightings divided by 106.

After fitting our model in Stan with the R interface RStan (v2.32.6, Stan Development Team, 2024), we generated 1000 samples from each of the four MCMC chains after a burn-in period of 1000 iterations. This simulated 4,000 draws from the posterior distributions of the mean duration of use and retention time at subnational, national, and continental scales.

Our subnational posterior estimates of the mean duration of use and retention time are then used in Section C in estimating the timing of mass campaigns. They are subsequently used as informative priors and are re-fitted to observed use and access data in Section D. This subsequent re-fitting process aids in reducing potential biases arising from the relative timings of surveys and campaigns as discussed above, and further reduces the influence of prior assumptions made in the hierarchical model described in Equations 11–13.

It should also be highlighted that while we have assumed an exponential loss function for the duration of use and access, other studies, including those by Bhatt et al., 2015 and Bertozzi-Villa et al., 2021, have utilised an ‘S-shaped’ smooth-compact loss function. This was originally developed for the net procurement planning tool, NetCALC (available at: http://www.networksmalaria.org/networks/netcalc) (Paintain et al., 2013). This functional form was fitted to net age distribution data (n>2500\begin{document}$n \gt 2500$\end{document} nets) across 12 surveys in Uganda prior to 2013 and was selected on the basis that the pooled observed age density peaked around 2 years and was sixfold greater than the density for newly distributed nets (Supplementary file 2, figure 2 in Paintain et al., 2013). Meanwhile for this study, discounting peaks at 12, 24, and 36 months (due to whole year rounding), the empirical age distribution broadly appears to be monotonically decreasing from month 6 onwards when pooled across all DHS surveys and countries included in this study (Appendix 2—figure 2a). However, the slight peak at month 6, which is twofold greater than at month 0, may be an artifact of MIS surveys often being conducted 6 months post-campaign, which would bias the sampled data to include more nets of this age. In light of potential survey artifacts and the largely monotonic decrease in net age, there was limited evidence against the use of an assumed exponential loss function from the data used in this study.

sec.title: 3.1 Estimating subnational timings
sec.p: Prior to estimating changes in use and access over time subnationally, we first sought to estimate the timings of subnational mass distribution campaigns. We assume that for all subnational regions i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} within a country ζ(i)\begin{document}$\zeta(i)$\end{document}, the kth\begin{document}$k^{\text{th}}$\end{document} national mass campaign is conducted within a given time interval, [rik,sik]∀i\begin{document}$\left[r_{ik},s_{ik}\right]\forall\, i$\end{document} where ζ(i)=ζ\begin{document}$\zeta(i)=\zeta$\end{document}. However, we do not necessarily assume that a national mass campaign occurs in synchrony across all regions.

Using data on the annual numbers of nets delivered to a country, Zζ(t)\begin{document}$Z_{\zeta}(t)$\end{document}, that was compiled by the The Alliance for Malaria Prevention, 2024 Net Mapping Project, we applied Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression (Nadaraya, 1964; Watson, 1964) to generate smoothened distributions, Zζ(t)\begin{document}$\mathcal{Z}_{\zeta}(t)$\end{document}. This was conducted using the ksmooth function from the R stats package (v4.3.2) for a bandwidth of 12 months due to the original resolution of the data being recorded annually (Appendix 3—figure 1a).

sec.p: If a net were selected randomly across space and time within a country ζ\begin{document}$\zeta$\end{document}, we treat Zζ(t)\begin{document}$\mathcal{Z}_{\zeta}(t)$\end{document} as an initial approximation of the probability of the month in which that net was received after normalisation. Under our assumption that mass campaigns are conducted within defined nationwide time intervals, we therefore consider the local minima of the density Zζ(i)(t)\begin{document}$\mathcal{Z}_{\zeta(i)}(t)$\end{document} to also be indicative of the local minima for the probability of a mass campaign occurring in any subnational region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} of country ζ(i)\begin{document}$\zeta(i)$\end{document} at those times. If the kth\begin{document}$k^{\text{th}}$\end{document} mass campaign in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} occurred at time τik\begin{document}$\tau_{ik}$\end{document}, we therefore define the range of possible values of τik\begin{document}$\tau_{ik}$\end{document} such that Zζ(i)(rik)\begin{document}$\mathcal{Z}_{\zeta(i)}(r_{ik})$\end{document} and Zζ(i)(sik)\begin{document}$\mathcal{Z}_{\zeta(i)}(s_{ik})$\end{document} are, respectively, the local minima of Zζ(i)\begin{document}$\mathcal{Z}_{\zeta(i)}$\end{document} immediately preceding and following mass campaign k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} given rik≤τik<sik\begin{document}$r_{ik}\leq\tau_{ik} \lt s_{ik}$\end{document} and sik=ri(k+1)\begin{document}$s_{ik}=r_{i(k+1)}$\end{document}.

To refine our estimates of when mass campaigns were likely to have occurred subnationally, we initially consider the recorded number of nets received by month in DHS surveys in subnational region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and normalise this to generate another density, Xi(t)\begin{document}$X_{i}(t)$\end{document} (Appendix 3—figure 1b). Given a total Ni\begin{document}$N_{i}$\end{document} nets were recorded across all surveys conducted in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}, we generated each density given the age, αil\begin{document}$\alpha_{il}$\end{document}, and survey date, hil\begin{document}$h_{il}$\end{document}, in months for each net l∈{1,…,Ni}\begin{document}$l\in\left\{1,\dots,N_{i}\right\}$\end{document}:(20)Xi(t)∼∑l=1Nif(t;αil,hil,wil)∑l=1Niwil\begin{document}$$\displaystyle X_{i}(t) \sim \frac{\sum_{l=1}^{N_i}f\left(t; \alpha_{il}, h_{il}, w_{il}\right)}{\sum_{l=1}^{N_i}w_{il}}$$\end{document}

such that wil\begin{document}$w_{il}$\end{document} is the DHS household survey weight for net l\begin{document}$l$\end{document} to correct for non-random probabilities of households being surveyed. However, since the density in Equation 20 is generated from nets that were observed in households, this density will be systematically biased by younger nets, since there will be a greater probability that an older net would have been discarded before it was recorded in a survey than a younger one. However, to account for months where no nets were recorded to have been distributed, we then generated a composite density with the stepwise normalised density, Zζ(i)(t)\begin{document}$Z_{\zeta(i)}(t)$\end{document}, that was proportional to the national number of nets distributed annually:(21)Vi(t)∝{Zζ(i)(t),if Wi(t)=0Wi(t),otherwise\begin{document}$$\displaystyle V_{i}(t) \propto \begin{cases} Z_{\zeta(i)}(t),&\text{if}\ W_{i}(t) = 0 \\ W_{i}(t),&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$\end{document}

We again conduct Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression on this composite density for each subnational region using the ksmooth function in R with a bandwidth of 12 months to generate smoothened densities, Vi(t)\begin{document}$\mathcal{V}_{i}(t)$\end{document} (Appendix 3—figure 1d). Our rationale for this is twofold; firstly, the composite density in Equation 21 is proportional to the number of annual nets distributed for some months; secondly, as the age distributions of nets for most subnational regions has notable peaks at 12, 24, and 36 months (Appendix 2—figure 2), it is probable that responses to this survey question were rounded to the nearest whole year by some participants.

After normalising the density Vi(t)\begin{document}$\mathcal{V}_{i}(t)$\end{document}, such that ∑tVi(t)=1\begin{document}$\sum_{t}\mathcal{V}_{i}(t)=1$\end{document}, this represents our best effort at capturing the probability of the month of distribution if a net is selected at random both in space and time within a subnational region. We then consider the probability density, Vik(t)\begin{document}$\mathcal{V}_{ik}(t)$\end{document}, of the distribution date of a net selected randomly conditional on that date being in the interval [rik,sik]\begin{document}$\left[r_{ik},s_{ik}\right]$\end{document} in which the kth\begin{document}$k^{\text{th}}$\end{document} mass distribution campaign occurred:Yik(t)∝{Vi(t),ifrik≤t<sik0,otherwise\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathcal{Y}_{ik}(t) \propto \begin{cases}\ \mathcal{V}_{i}(t),&\text{if}\ r_{ik}\leq t \lt s_{ik}\\ \ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$\end{document}

After discretising this density by month and by normalising such that ∑tYik(t)=1\begin{document}$\sum_{t}\mathcal{Y}_{ik}(t)=1$\end{document}, we then treat Yik(t)\begin{document}$\mathcal{Y}_{ik}(t)$\end{document} as a proxy for the probability of mass campaign k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} occurring at time τik\begin{document}$\tau_{ik}$\end{document} in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}:P[τik=t]=Yik(t)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbb{P}\left[\tau_{ik}= t\right] = \mathcal{Y}_{ik}(t)$$\end{document}

The expected value of the timing of a mass campaign is therefore estimated from:(22)E[τik]=∑τ=riksik−1τYik(τ)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{ik}\right] = \sum_{\tau = r_{ik}}^{s_{ik} - 1}\tau \mathcal{Y}_{ik}(\tau) $$\end{document}

To account for uncertainty in the timing of mass campaigns, we then calculate the variance around the timing of each mass campaign:(23)Var[τik]=E[τik2]−E[τik]2\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{Var}\big[ \tau_{ik}\big] = \mathbb{E}\big[ \tau_{ik}^{2} \big] - \mathbb{E}\big[ \tau_{ik}\big]^{2} $$\end{document}
GivenE[τik2]=∑τ=riksik−1τ2Yik(τ)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{ik}^{2}\right] = \sum_{\tau = r_{ik}}^{s_{ik} - 1}\tau^{2} \mathcal{Y}_{ik}(\tau)$$\end{document}

While this approach represented our best effort at capturing the central tendency of the subnational timings of mass campaigns, the variances calculated from Equation 23 are likely to overestimate the degree of uncertainty in campaign timing. For example, for variance around the period of the 2019 mass campaign in Est, Burkina Faso, is far greater than in 2016 (Appendix 3—figure 1d). However, this is potentially driven by a DHS survey being conducted at the end of 2021, which resulted in a notable number of ITNs being reported as 24 and 36 months old, due to rounding to the nearest whole year. We therefore propose that the peaks in the composite density in Appendix 3—figure 1d are primarily driven by whole year rounding, which has resulted in a large variance in the smoothened density that potentially overinflates the uncertainty in the timing of the 2019 mass campaign.

Due to the potential of overestimating the uncertainty in the timings of mass campaigns due to whole year rounding in survey responses, we rank the variances calculated from Equation 23 for all mass campaigns in all regions. We then split these into tertiles of equal size based on the variances calculated from Equation 23 and assign standard deviations for the timings of mass campaign k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}, στik\begin{document}$\sigma_{\tau ik}$\end{document} of one, two and three to represent mass campaigns where there is low, medium and high uncertainty in the timing of mass campaigns. We then approximate the uncertainty around our central estimates with a truncated-normal (TN) density with upper and lower bounds set at three standard deviations from the expected value:(24)τik∣Xi,Zζ(i)∼ approx TN⁡(τ¯ik,στik2,aik,bik)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau_{i k} \mid X_i, Z_{\zeta(i)} \stackrel{\text { approx }}{\sim} \operatorname{TN}\left(\bar{\tau}_{i k}, \sigma_{\tau i k}^2, a_{i k}, b_{i k}\right)$$\end{document}

whereaik=τ¯ik−3στik\begin{document}$$\displaystyle a_{ik}= \bar{\tau}_{ik}- 3\sigma_{\tau ik} $$\end{document}bik=τ¯ik+3στik\begin{document}$$\displaystyle b_{ik}= \bar{\tau}_{ik}+ 3\sigma_{\tau ik} $$\end{document}

and τ¯ik=E[τik]\begin{document}$\bar{\tau}_{ik}=\mathbb{E}\left[\tau_{ik}\right]$\end{document} from Equation 22. This gives a range of proposed dates for the area which is desirable as campaigns are likely to be spread out over a period given the geographical scale of the area and the considerable logistics involved. The proposed timings of mass campaigns were verified where possible though discussion with interested parties nationally and internationally, though further work to record the subnational timings of mass campaigns is encouraged.

sec.title: 3.2 Time since the most recent campaign
sec.p: If the time of the last campaign (ϕij\begin{document}$\phi_{ij}$\end{document}) in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} before a survey at time tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document} was known, then we could directly infer the months since the last campaign:(25)mij=tj−ϕij\begin{document}$$\displaystyle m_{ij}= t_{j} - \phi_{ij}$$\end{document}

In contexts where national malaria programmes or other stakeholders have knowledge of the timings of mass campaigns (i.e. when there is no uncertainty in ϕij\begin{document}$\phi_{ij}$\end{document}), the methodology can be adapted by deterministically evaluating the time since the last campaign (Equation 25) for each time point. However, the timings (τik\begin{document}$\tau_{ik}$\end{document}) of each kth\begin{document}$k^{\text{th}}$\end{document} campaign in each region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} are unknown random variables. Although we do not know their exact timings, we captured our uncertainty of them previously through Equation 24. Before we can probabilistically represent the months since the last mass campaign, we need to probabilistically estimate the timing of the last campaign relative to each time point tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document} for each region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}. Before proceeding, we note that for all regions, the supports [aik,bik]\begin{document}$\left[a_{ik},b_{ik}\right]$\end{document} of the probability distribution (Equation 24) for the timing of each kth\begin{document}$k^{\text{th}}$\end{document} campaign are non-overlapping:τik∈[aik,bik]for all k≥1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tau_{ik}\in [a_{ik}, b_{ik}] \qquad \text{for all }k \geq 1$$\end{document}
whereai(k+1)>bikfor all k≥1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle a_{i(k+1)} \gt b_{ik}\qquad \text{for all }k \geq 1$$\end{document}

For times tj<ai1\begin{document}$t_{j} \lt a_{i1}$\end{document} that precede the support [ai1,bi1]\begin{document}$\left[a_{i1},b_{i1}\right]$\end{document} of the distribution for the first campaign, we therefore will have assumed a 100% probability that there was no preceding campaign. Therefore, the probability of using any net here is equal to the probability of using a continuously distributed net, pij=dij\begin{document}$p_{ij}=d_{ij}$\end{document}, as per Equation 31. We can also represent this as a unit point mass (δ−∞\begin{document}$\delta_{-\infty}$\end{document}) for a campaign occurring at t=−∞\begin{document}$t=-\infty$\end{document}, since limϕij→−∞mij=∞\begin{document}$\lim_{\phi_{ij}\to-\infty}m_{ij}=\infty$\end{document} from Equation 25 and limmij→∞cij=0\begin{document}$\lim_{m_{ij}\to\infty}c_{ij}=0$\end{document} from Equation 35. The distribution of the timing of the last campaign conditional on a 100% probability of there being no preceding campaign to tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document} is therefore given by:(26)ϕij∣(tj<ai1) ∼ δ−∞\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \phi_{ij}\mid \left(t_{j} \lt a_{i1}\right) \ \sim \ \delta_{-\infty}$$\end{document}

For the remainder of this section, given some time tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document}, we specifically use k\begin{document}$k$\end{document} to denote the index of the campaign in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} with an uncertainty window [aik,bik]\begin{document}$[a_{ik},b_{ik}]$\end{document} that either contains (aik≤tj<bik\begin{document}$a_{ik}\leq t_{j} \lt b_{ik}$\end{document}) or immediately precedes (bik≤tj<ai(k+1)\begin{document}$b_{ik}\leq t_{j} \lt a_{i(k+1)}$\end{document}) time tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document}. For times between the supports of the distribution (Equation 24) describing the timing of the last kth\begin{document}$k^{\text{th}}$\end{document} campaign and the next (k+1)th\begin{document}$(k+1)^{\text{th}}$\end{document} campaign (i.e. when bik≤tj<ai(k+1)\begin{document}$b_{ik}\leq t_{j} \lt a_{i(k+1)}$\end{document}), we will have assumed a 100% probability that the last campaign relative to tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document} will be the kth\begin{document}$k^{\text{th}}$\end{document} campaign. In this case, the probability distribution of the timing of the last campaign is the same as the timing of the kth\begin{document}$k^{\text{th}}$\end{document} campaign:(27)ϕij∣(bik≤tj<ai(k+1))∼τik\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \phi_{ij}\mid \left(b_{ik}\leq t_{j} \lt a_{i(k+1)}\right) \sim \tau_{ik}$$\end{document}

Now, let Fik\begin{document}$F_{ik}$\end{document} be the cumulative distribution function of the truncated normal distribution for the timing of the kth\begin{document}$k^{\text{th}}$\end{document} campaign (Equation 24). For times within the uncertainty window of the first campaign (when ai1≤tj<bi1\begin{document}$a_{i1}\leq t_{j} \lt b_{i1}$\end{document}), there will be some probability Fi1(tj)\begin{document}$F_{i1}(t_{j})$\end{document} that the first campaign was the most recent; the remaining probability would be that there was no preceding campaign. In this case, the probability distribution of the timing of the last campaign will be:(28)ϕij∣(ai1≤tj<bi1)∼{τi1∣(τi1≤tj)with probability Fi1(tj),δ−∞with probability 1−Fi1(tj).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \phi_{ij}\mid \left(a_{i1}\leq t_{j} \lt b_{i1}\right) \, \sim \, \begin{cases}\tau_{i1}\mid (\tau_{i1}\leq t_{j})&\text{with probability }F_{i1}(t_{j}), \\ \delta_{-\infty}&\text{with probability }1-F_{i1}(t_{j}).\end{cases} $$\end{document}

Extending this to the general case, for times within the uncertainty window of any other campaign (k≥2\begin{document}$k\geq 2$\end{document}), there will be some probability Fik(tj)\begin{document}$F_{ik}(t_{j})$\end{document} that campaign was the most recent, with the remaining probability that the earlier campaign was the most recent:(29)ϕij∣(aik≤tj<bik,k≥2) ∼ {τik∣(τik≤tj)with probability Fik(tj),τi(k−1)with probability 1−Fik(tj).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \phi_{ij}\mid \left(a_{ik}\leq t_{j} \lt b_{ik}, k \geq 2 \right) \ \sim \ \begin{cases}\tau_{ik}\mid (\tau_{ik}\leq t_{j})&\text{with probability }F_{ik}(t_{j}), \\ \tau_{i(k-1)}&\text{with probability }1-F_{ik}(t_{j}).\end{cases} $$\end{document}

From Equations 26–29, we can therefore describe the probability distribution of the timing of the last campaign relative to any time tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document} in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} as follows:(30)ϕij∣tj∼{δ−∞,tj<ai1,τi1∣(τi1≤tj) with probability Fi1(tj), otherwise δ−∞,ai1≤tj<bi1,τik∣(τik≤tj) with probability Fik(tj), otherwise τi(k−1),aik≤tj<bik,k≥2,τik,bik≤tj<ai(k+1).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \phi_{ij}\mid t_{j} \, \sim \, \begin{cases}\delta_{-\infty},&t_{j} \lt a_{i1}, \\ \tau_{i1}\mid (\tau_{i1}\le t_{j}) \text{ with probability }F_{i1}(t_{j}), \text{ otherwise }\delta_{-\infty},&a_{i1}\le t_{j} \lt b_{i1}, \\ \tau_{ik}\mid (\tau_{ik}\le t_{j}) \text{ with probability }F_{ik}(t_{j}), \text{ otherwise }\tau_{i(k-1)},&a_{ik}\le t_{j} \lt b_{ik},\; k \ge 2, \\ \tau_{ik},&b_{ik}\le t_{j} \lt a_{i(k+1)}.\end{cases} $$\end{document}
Then, given Equation 30, the months since the last campaign for any general tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document} can also be treated as a random variable and inferred directly from Equation 25.

sec.title: 4. Historical use and access
sec.p: The model presented in this section describes how we estimated historical trends in access. Aside from fitting the model to the number of individuals who used nets, uij\begin{document}$u_{ij}$\end{document}, instead of those who had access, aij\begin{document}$a_{ij}$\end{document}, in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} at time tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document}, the methodology is otherwise identical to how we estimated historical trends in use.

sec.title: 4.1. Core model structure
sec.p: An ITN is assumed to provide access for up to two people within the same household, except where more than two individuals were recorded as having slept under the same net; in such cases, an ITN is assumed to provide access to all individuals who slept under it the previous night. When fewer than two people sleep under an ITN, access is allocated at random among the remaining household members who did not use a net. When more than one ITN can provide access to an individual who did not sleep under one, the net deemed to provide access is also assigned at random.

Given the first mass campaign in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} occurs at time τi1\begin{document}$\tau_{i1}$\end{document} (Equation 24), we compartmentalise the proportion of the population with access (pij\begin{document}$p_{ij}$\end{document}) into access provided by campaign-distributed ITNs (cij\begin{document}$c_{ij}$\end{document}) and continuously distributed ITNs (dij\begin{document}$d_{ij}$\end{document}):(31)pij={dij,if tj<τi1cij+dij,otherwise\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p_{ij}= \begin{cases}d_{ij}&, \text{if }t_{j} \lt \tau_{i1}\\ c_{ij}+ d_{ij}&, \text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$\end{document}

We then denote pij0\begin{document}$p_{ij}^{0}$\end{document} as the proportion with access immediately following a mass campaign. We assume this exhibits logistic-type growth over time towards some saturation threshold, ψi\begin{document}$\psi_{i}$\end{document}:(32)pij0=ψilogit−1(βi0+βittj)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p_{ij}^{0} = \psi_{i} \text{logit}^{-1}\left(\beta_{i}^{0} + \beta_{i}^{t} t_{j} \right) $$\end{document}

Immediately following any campaign, when pij=pij0\begin{document}$p_{ij}=p_{ij}^{0}$\end{document}, we assume the proportion of access attributable to campaign-distributed ITNs, relative to access from any ITN, is constant and given by qi0\begin{document}$q_{i}^{0}$\end{document}. The proportions of the population with access to campaign-distributed and continuously distributed ITNs immediately following a campaign are, respectively:(33)cij0=qi0pij0\begin{document}$$\displaystyle c_{ij}^{0}= q_{i}^{0} p_{ij}^{0} $$\end{document}(34)dij=(1−qi0)pij0\begin{document}$$\displaystyle d_{ij}= \left(1-q_{i}^{0}\right)p_{ij}^{0} $$\end{document}
Since qij0\begin{document}$q_{ij}^{0}$\end{document} is assumed to be constant, we also implicitly assume access to continuously distributed ITNs also exhibits logistic-type growth.

Where cij0=cij\begin{document}$c_{ij}^{0}=c_{ij}$\end{document} when the number of months following a mass campaign, mij=0\begin{document}$m_{ij}=0$\end{document}. We have also implicitly assumed continually distributed nets are replenished in the population such that the proportion with access to them grows logistically over time since dij∝pij0\begin{document}$d_{ij}\propto p_{ij}^{0}$\end{document}.

However, as mass campaigns are conducted periodically, given we assume ITNs are discarded with a constant hazard rate, the proportion with access to a campaign-sourced ITN will decay over time following the last campaign:(35)cij=cij0exp(−λimij)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle c_{ij}= c_{ij}^{0} \, \text{exp}\left(-\lambda_{i} m_{ij}\right) $$\end{document}

If ITNs are distributed without replacement (an assumption which is later relaxed), then the inverse of the decay parameter in Equation 35, λ−1\begin{document}$\lambda^{-1}$\end{document}, is equal to the mean retention time. Given the proportion of the overall population with access to campaign ITNs decays over time, it follows that the proportion with access to a campaign ITN relative to the proportion with access to any ITN (qij\begin{document}$q_{ij}$\end{document}) will decrease over time following the last mass campaign:(36)qij=cijpij\begin{document}$$\displaystyle q_{ij}= \frac{c_{ij}}{p_{ij}}$$\end{document}

sec.title: 4.2. Prior distributions
sec.p: To fit our model, we use our previous posterior estimates of mean retention times given observed net ages to inform strongly informative priors (Equation 37) of the mean retention time, with either non-informative or regularising priors for other parameters:(37)λi−1∼N>0(μλi,σλi2)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \lambda_{i}^{-1}\sim \text{N}_{ \gt 0}\left(\mu_{\lambda i}, \sigma_{\lambda i}^{2} \right) $$\end{document}(38)β^i0∼N(0,0.1)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat{\beta}_{i}^{0}\sim \text{N}\left(0, 0.1 \right) $$\end{document}(39)β^it∼N>0(σtt¯,0.1)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \hat{\beta}_{i}^{t}\sim \text{N}_{ \gt 0}\left(\frac{\sigma_{t}}{\bar{t}}, 0.1 \right) $$\end{document}(40)ψi∼Beta(0.5,0.5)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \psi_{i}\sim \text{Beta}\left(0.5, 0.5 \right) $$\end{document}(41)qi0∼Beta(0.5,0.5)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle q_{i}^{0}\sim \text{Beta}\left(0.5, 0.5\right) $$\end{document}(42)αi0∼Exp(10−3)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \alpha_{i}^{0}\sim \text{Exp}(10^{-3}) $$\end{document}

Given the posterior mean and variance of the mean ITN retention time conditional on observed ITN ages:μλi=E[γi−1|αi]\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mu_{\lambda i}= \mathbb{E}\left[ \gamma_{i}^{-1}\big| \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i} \right] $$\end{document}σλi2=Var[γi−1|αi]\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sigma_{\lambda i}^{2}= \text{Var}\left[ \gamma_{i}^{-1}\big| \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i} \right] $$\end{document}

which are estimated from the sampled posterior distribution of mean ITN retention from the hierarchical model (Equations 11 and 18) described in Initial estimation of ITN retention times:π(γi−1|αi)∝π(γi−1)π(αi|γi−1)=π(γi−1)∏l=1Miπ(αil|γi−1)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \pi\left(\gamma_{i}^{-1}\,\big|\, \boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}\right) \propto \pi\left(\gamma_{i}^{-1}\right) \pi\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i} \,\big| \,\gamma_{i}^{-1}\right) = \pi\left(\gamma_{i}^{-1}\right) \prod_{l=1}^{M_{i}}\pi\left(\alpha_{il}\,\big|\, \gamma_{i}^{-1}\right)$$\end{document}

where αi={αi1,…,αil,…,αiMi}\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{i}=\{\alpha_{i1},\dots,\alpha_{il},\dots,\alpha_{iM_{i}}\}$\end{document} is the vector of ages of ITNs providing access in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}. Here, Mi\begin{document}$M_{i}$\end{document} denotes the total observed number of ITNs providing access of any age r\begin{document}$r$\end{document} after correcting for DHS sample weights such that Mi=∑rMir\begin{document}$M_{i}=\sum_{r}M_{ir}$\end{document} (Equation 19).

Meanwhile, survey times were standardised such that t^j=(tj−t¯)/σt\begin{document}$\hat{t}_{j}=\left(t_{j}-\bar{t}\right)/\sigma_{t}$\end{document} with E[t^]=0\begin{document}$\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{t}\right]=0$\end{document} and Var[t^]=1\begin{document}$\text{Var}\left[\hat{t}\right]=1$\end{document}. Therefore, on the logit scale of the probability of access immediately following a mass campaign relative to its maximum value (i.e. logit(pij0/ψi)\begin{document}$\text{logit}\,(p^{0}_{ij}/\psi_{i})$\end{document}), the intercept and slope parameters on the original time scale are therefore given by:βi0=β^i0−β^itσtt¯\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \beta_{i}^{0}= \hat{\beta}_{i}^{0} - \frac{\hat{\beta}_{i}^{t}}{\sigma_{t}}\, \bar{t}$$\end{document}βit=β^itσt\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \beta_{i}^{t}= \frac{\hat{\beta}_{i}^{t}}{\sigma_{t}} $$\end{document}

Priors on the standardised coefficients (Equations 38 and 39) were chosen to provide regularisation against implausibly abrupt changes on the standardised scale, while non-informative Beta(0.5,0.5)\begin{document}$\text{Beta}\,(0.5,0.5)$\end{document} priors were used for the maximum probability of access (Equation 40) and the conditional probability access is provided by a campaign-sourced ITN immediately following a campaign (Equation 41).

Finally, we use a regularising Exponential(10−3) prior for the overdispersion parameter (αi0\begin{document}$\alpha_{i}^{0}$\end{document}), which controls subregional heterogeneity in access and is discussed further in Section D. A flat or more diffuse prior was avoided, as it would assign disproportionate weight to extremely large values of αi0\begin{document}$\alpha_{i}^{0}$\end{document}. Our choice centres prior belief on low overdispersion (E[αi0]=1000\begin{document}$\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{i}^{0}]=1000$\end{document} a priori); this corresponds to a maximum subregional standard deviation in access of approximately 1.6%. However, it retains support for substantially lower values of αi0\begin{document}$\alpha_{i}^{0}$\end{document}, which correspond to higher overdispersion and greater subnational variability in access, where suggested by the data.

sec.title: 4.3. Likelihood specification
sec.p: Before formulating our likelihood model, we note there are two sources of data from the DHS that can be used, in addition to the previous posterior inference made on retention times given the surveyed ages of nets.

Firstly, given nij\begin{document}$n_{ij}$\end{document} surveyed individuals in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} at time tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document}, we can construct the likelihood from the probability of observing the number of individuals with access, aij\begin{document}$a_{ij}$\end{document}, given our parameters:(43)aij∣p~ij∼Binomial(nij,p~ij)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle a_{ij}\mid \tilde{p}_{ij}\sim \text{Binomial}\left(n_{ij}, \tilde{p}_{ij}\right) $$\end{document}

where the probability of having access to an ITN at time tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document} is denoted by p~ij\begin{document}$\tilde{p}_{ij}$\end{document}. However, we do not assume this is equal to the proportion of the population (pij\begin{document}$p_{ij}$\end{document}) with access to ITNs for all individuals. There is likely to be greater variability in access to, and indeed use of, ITNs both within subnational regions and over time; for example, differing access between districts within subnational regions or differing use between rainy and dry seasons. These potential additional sources of uncertainty are not directly accounted for in our discrete-time model of historical access (and use) (Equations 31 and 36). Focusing again on access, to account for differences in the probability of access between individuals in the same region, we assume the probability of access at a given point in time can be described by a Beta distribution:(44)p~ij∼Beta(αi0pij,αi0(1−pij))\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tilde{p}_{ij}\sim \text{Beta}\left(\alpha^{0}_{i} p_{ij}, \alpha^{0}_{i}(1-p_{ij})\right) $$\end{document}

Equations 43 and 44 can then be decomposed to a Beta-Binomial likelihood. The mean probability of individual access across a region at a given point in time is then equal to the overall proportion with access:E[p~ij]=pij\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[\tilde{p}_{ij}] = p_{ij}$$\end{document}

Meanwhile, the overdispersion parameter, αi0\begin{document}$\alpha_{i}^{0}$\end{document} (unrelated to the notation for ITN age), controls the variability of the probability of individual access around the mean:Var[p~ij]=pij(1−pij)αi0+1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \text{Var}[\tilde{p}_{ij}] = \frac{p_{ij}(1-p_{ij})}{\alpha_{i}^{0}+1}$$\end{document}

Such that smaller values of αi0\begin{document}$\alpha_{i}^{0}$\end{document} imply greater variability in the probability of individual access. While this variance will change as a function of the proportion with access, we assume the overdispersion parameter is constant for each region over time.

Secondly, given those individuals with access, we can construct the likelihood that nets providing access were distributed through campaigns, given the total number of ITNs that were recorded, or imputed, as having originated from campaigns, yij\begin{document}$y_{ij}$\end{document}:(45)aij∣p~ij∼Binomial(nij,p~ij)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle a_{ij}\mid \tilde{p}_{ij}\sim \text{Binomial}\left(n_{ij}, \tilde{p}_{ij}\right)$$\end{document}

For each ITN l\begin{document}$l$\end{document} that provided access in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}, we assign an indicator variable, υil\begin{document}$\upsilon_{il}$\end{document}, depending on whether the net originated from a campaign (υil=1\begin{document}$\upsilon_{il}=1$\end{document}) or from continuous distribution (υil=0\begin{document}$\upsilon_{il}=0$\end{document}). For the purposes of this study, we treat an ITN with any recorded source other than a campaign as having originated from continuous distribution channels. Sources either recorded as missing or ‘NA’ in DHS surveys are treated as missing data, and are denoted with υil′\begin{document}$\upsilon^{\prime}_{il}$\end{document}. Letting y¯i\begin{document}$\bar{y}_{i}$\end{document} be the observed proportion of ITNs from campaigns that provided access in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document}, for each net where the source was not recorded, we probabilistically impute whether they originated from campaigns:υil′∼Bernoulli(y¯i)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \upsilon'_{il}\sim \text{Bernoulli}\left(\bar{y}_{i}\right)$$\end{document}

sec.title: 4.4. ITN retention under random allocation
sec.p: The model described in Equations 31–35 describes how use and access change over time in different subnational regions. In itself, this makes no assumptions on whether the probability an individual will receive a net is independent of whether an individual already has access to, or is currently using, a net. If ITNs are assumed to be distributed without replacement such that they are only distributed to individuals without access to a net, then the inverse of the decay parameter λ\begin{document}$\lambda$\end{document} (Equation 35) will be equal to the mean retention time of a net (or the mean duration of use when the model is applied in that context). However, for simulating transmission dynamics, we make the conservative assumption that ITNs are distributed randomly to the population. Therefore, we assume individuals are equally likely to start using, or gain access to, a net following a campaign or continuous distribution event irrespective of whether they are currently using or have access to one. As before, we will describe the remainder of this section in the context of access, though the same also applies for use.

While our use and access model Equations 31–35 is discretised by month to facilitate fitting to DHS data, our transmission dynamics model is simulated with the malariasimulation (v1.6.0) R package (Charles et al., 2024), which discretises a continuous-time model over daily timesteps. The transmission dynamics model only explicitly models use, and so the remainder of this section is described in that context.

Dropping region-specific subscripts for notational ease, the continuous-time model for the proportion of the population with use, which we wish to replicate in our transmission dynamics model is:(46)p(t)=c(t)+d(t)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p(t)= c(t) + d(t) $$\end{document}(47)c(t)=q0p0(t)exp⁡(−λim(t))\begin{document}$$\displaystyle c(t)= q^{0} p^{0}(t) \exp \left(-\lambda_{i} m(t) \right) $$\end{document}(48)d(t)=(1−q0)p0(t)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle d(t)= \left(1 - q^{0} \right) p^{0}(t) $$\end{document}(49)p0(t)=ψilogit−1(βi0+βittj)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p^{0}(t)= \psi_{i} \, \text{logit}^{-1}(\beta_{i}^{0} + \beta_{i}^{t} t_{j}) $$\end{document}
where all variables and parameters are as defined under the discrete-time model for the period January 2008 to December 2024, with time dependence explicitly indicated.

To reduce computational overheads, we simulate the distribution of ITNs at the start of every month in our transmission dynamics model. If we consider a region with no mass campaign distribution (when q0=0\begin{document}$q^{0}=0$\end{document}), then if there is a proportion d0=d\begin{document}$d_{0}=d$\end{document} of the population using ITNs at the start of some month, then some small Δt\begin{document}$\Delta t$\end{document} immediately prior to the start of the next month the proportion of the population using ITNs will be:d1−Δt=d0exp⁡(−Λ)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle d_{1-\Delta t}= d_{0} \exp (-\Lambda)$$\end{document}

where Λ−1\begin{document}$\Lambda^{-1}$\end{document} months is the mean duration of use (under our assumption of random allocation of ITNs) and the underlying logistic-type growth in continuous use of nets is assumed to be sufficiently small over 1 month (i.e. d⁢p0/d⁢t≈0\begin{document}$\nicefrac{{dp^{0}}}{{dt}}\approx 0$\end{document}). If we then assume random allocation of nets at the start of the next month, for the expected use of ITNs to reach the same level as the preceding month such that E[d1]=d0\begin{document}$\mathbb{E}[d_{1}]=d_{0}$\end{document}, we require ITNs to be distributed to a proportion Δd\begin{document}$\Delta d$\end{document} of the population where:Δd=d0−d1−Δt1−d1−Δt\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Delta d = \frac{d_{0} - d_{1-\Delta t}}{1 - d_{1-\Delta t}}$$\end{document}

We now consider the counterfactual with mass campaigns occurring in the same region. If a campaign is conducted at some month (m=0\begin{document}$m=0$\end{document}) such that use immediately after it is p0\begin{document}$p_{0}$\end{document}, then by the end of that month (m=1−Δt\begin{document}$m=1-\Delta t$\end{document}) it follows that use would be:p1−Δt=p0exp⁡(−Λ)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p_{1-\Delta t}= p_{0} \exp (-\Lambda)$$\end{document}

This can alternatively be described by the following initial value problem, again assuming underlying logistic-type growth occurs over much longer timescales than the decay in use following a campaign:∂p^∂m=−Λp^,p^(0)=p0,0≤m<1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{\partial \hat{p}}{\partial m}= - \Lambda \hat{p}, \quad \hat{p}(0) = p_{0}, \quad 0 \leq m \lt 1$$\end{document}

Then, at the start of the next month (m=1\begin{document}$m=1$\end{document}), following a top-up distribution of ITNs through continuous channels that are randomly allocated to the population, the expected population use is:(50)E[p1]=p1−Δt+Δd(1−p1−Δt)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[p_{1}] = p_{1-\Delta t}+ \Delta d (1 - p_{1-\Delta t}) $$\end{document}

Following substitution and some algebra, it can be shown that if the mean duration of use is assumed to be the same when ITNs are distributed with replacement as without (i.e. λ−1=Λ−1\begin{document}$\lambda^{-1}=\Lambda^{-1}$\end{document}), then the expected population use (Equation 50) following a continuous distribution top-up will underestimate the target value (Equation 46) since E[p1]<p(1)\begin{document}$\mathbb{E}[p_{1}] \lt p(1)$\end{document}. An improved approximation can instead be found by approximating the change in use from Equation 46 as an exponential decay given:∂p∂m=−λc\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{\partial p}{\partial m}= -\lambda c$$\end{document}

and so letting:∂p∂m≈∂p^∂m⟹Λ(m)≈λc(m)p^(m)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{\partial p}{\partial m}\approx \frac{\partial \hat{p}}{\partial m}\quad \implies \quad \Lambda(m) \approx \frac{\lambda c(m)}{\hat{p}(m)}$$\end{document}
Then, applying this approximation immediately following a campaign:Λ=Λ(0)≈λq0\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Lambda = \Lambda(0) \approx \lambda q^{0}$$\end{document}

Therefore, the mean duration of use (under the assumption of random allocation of use with replacement) can be estimated from:(51)Λ−1≈(λq0)−1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \Lambda^{-1}\approx (\lambda q^{0})^{-1}$$\end{document}

Although this is still an approximation, it can be shown to be a closer one than Λ−1≈λ−1\begin{document}$\Lambda^{-1}\approx\lambda^{-1}$\end{document} provided the following condition is satisfied:p0>K\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p^{0} \gt K$$\end{document}
whereK=λd2log⁡([1−d(1−exp⁡(−λ))]−1)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle K = \frac{\lambda d}{2 \log \left(\left[ 1 - d \left(1 - \exp(-\lambda) \right) \right]^{-1}\right)}$$\end{document}
and for small λ:K≈12\begin{document}$$\displaystyle K \approx \frac{1}{2}$$\end{document}

which is approximately true when λ is restricted to realistic values; for example, it can be shown 0.5051<K<0.5105\begin{document}$0.5051 \lt K \lt 0.5105$\end{document} for all possible values of d\begin{document}$d$\end{document} when λ=124 month−1\begin{document}$\lambda=\frac{{1}}{{24}}\text{ month}^{-1}$\end{document}. Over the recent period of interest (i.e. since December 2024), use immediately following a campaign is likely to be notably greater than 50% in all regions and so we report our estimated mean durations of ITN use for different regions using the approximation given by Equation 51. The same approach is also repeated in the context of access to give estimates of the mean ITN retention time.

sec.title: 5.1. Over-reporting of ITN use
sec.p: While we fitted the discrete-time model of historical access and use directly to observed DHS data, hereafter we accounted for the potential of self-reported ITN use through DHS surveys to be greater than objectively measured use. A meta-analysis by Krezanoski et al., 2018 estimated self-reported ITN use is typically 8% (95% CI: 3, 13) higher than the true value or a 13.6% relative overestimation. As the majority of regions were estimated to have levels of use greater than 90% immediately following a campaign by 2024 under our model, and since use following mass campaigns is estimated to have meaningfully increased over 2018–2024 for most regions, we take a conservative approach in accounting for over-reporting and purposefully treat the absolute values estimated by Krezanoski et al., 2018 as relative values to the reported use. The scaled probability of use, p~ij\begin{document}$\tilde{p}_{ij}$\end{document} is herein assumed to be:p~ij=(1−ϵi)pij\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \tilde{p}_{ij}= \left(1 - \epsilon_{i} \right) p_{ij}$$\end{document}
where(52)ϵi∼N>0(0.08,(0.051.96)2)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \epsilon_{i} \sim \text{N}_{ \gt 0}\left(0.08, \left(\frac{0.05}{1.96}\right)^{2} \right) $$\end{document}

This over-reporting assumption is applied for both campaign-distributed and continuously distributed ITNs. While we do not assume a similar systematic discrepancy between surveyed access and true access, the over-reporting assumption applied to use is accounted for in our calculations of use given access.

sec.title: 5.2. Region-specific calibration
sec.p: Future projections were conducted using malariasimulation (v1.6.0) (Charles et al., 2024), which encodes an individual-based P. falciparum transmission dynamics model. The core structure and parameterisation of the model are described in Griffin et al., 2014; Griffin et al., 2010 and are detailed in full at https://mrc-ide.github.io/malariasimulation/index.html. Aside from ITN-interventions, transmission dynamics models were calibrated for rural and urban settings in each subnational unit using the site (v0.2.2) (https://mrc-ide.github.io/site/) (Winskill, 2024b) R package, which has compiled location specific data from multiple sources for 2000–2024. site characterises local human population structure from WorldPop population estimates, and vector abundance and distribution by species from Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) estimates (Winskill, 2024b). site has also compiled treatment rates and coverage of non-ITN interventions, including indoor residual spraying of insecticide (IRS), seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC), drug treatment, and vaccination from historical estimates by the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP), DHS STATcompiler, ACCESS-SMC, the SMC Alliance and the Malaria Vaccine Implementation Programme (Winskill, 2024b). Model seasonality is characterised (Winskill, 2024b) by fitting Fourier series to CHIRPS daily rainfall data for each administrative-one unit. A linear relationship following a 30-day delay between the rainfall Fourier series and larval carrying capacity is assumed in each location following White et al., 2011. Administrative-one level estimates of pyrethroid resistance have been estimated using spatio-temporally distributed bioassay mortality data (Winskill, 2022).

After accounting for population structure and non-ITN interventions, we calibrated the baseline transmission intensity (i.e. prior to the introduction of control interventions) using the cali (v1.0.8) R package (https://mrc-ide.github.io/cali/) (Winskill, 2024a). cali utilises an optimisation algorithm to minimise the sum of absolute differences between a desired prevalence series and one predicted by a model. For this process we fitted our historical model estimates of PfPR2−10 to median estimates of the mean annual PfPR2−10 from the Malaria Atlas Project over 2005–2024 that were compiled by the site package (Winskill, 2024b). Since the relationship between baseline EIR and PfPR2−10 here is specific to malariasimulation, MAP uncertainty estimates were not propagated through to our estimates in baseline EIR since these would not faithfully represent its true uncertainty. As a means of validation, we compared our model estimates of PfPR6−59mo to estimates from DHS surveys (e.g. Figure 2B). We have also quantified the uncertainty in the estimate of the true PfPR6−59mo values (Pij\begin{document}$\mathcal{P}_{ij}$\end{document}) attributable to the number of children tested in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} at time tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document}. Using a conjugate Beta-Binomial model with a non-informative Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior, the posterior distribution of P\begin{document}$\mathcal{P}$\end{document} is:Pij∣(xij+,xij−)∼Beta(xij++0.5,ijx−+0.5)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathcal{P}_{ij}\mid (x_{ij}^{+}, x_{ij}^{-}) \sim \text{Beta}\left(x_{ij}^{+} + 0.5,_{ij}x^{-} + 0.5 \right)$$\end{document}

where xij+=∑l=1nij+wijl\begin{document}$x_{ij}^{+}=\sum_{l=1}^{n_{ij}^{+}}w_{ijl}$\end{document}, and xij−=∑l=1nij−wijl\begin{document}$x_{ij}^{-}=\sum_{l=1}^{n_{ij}^{-}}w_{ijl}$\end{document}, given nij+\begin{document}$n_{ij}^{+}$\end{document} and nij−\begin{document}$n_{ij}^{-}$\end{document} are the number of 6- to 59-month-olds who tested positive and negative, respectively, at time tj\begin{document}$t_{j}$\end{document} in region i\begin{document}$i$\end{document} and wijl\begin{document}$w_{ijl}$\end{document} is the scaled DHS sample weight for child l\begin{document}$l$\end{document} such that xij++xij−=nij++nij−\begin{document}$x_{ij}^{+}+x_{ij}^{-}=n_{ij}^{+}+n_{ij}^{-}$\end{document}.

sec.title: 5.3. ITN efficacy parameters
sec.p: The insecticidal activity of an ITN is assumed to decay at a constant rate, γN\begin{document}$\gamma_{N}$\end{document}. Conditional on a feeding attempt on a human using an ITN of age α, the probability that a mosquito successfully feeds (sN)\begin{document}$\left(s_{N}\right)$\end{document}, or is repelled (rN)\begin{document}$\left(r_{N}\right)$\end{document} or killed (dN)\begin{document}$\left(d_{N}\right)$\end{document} by that ITN is described by:(53)rN=(rN0−rNM)exp⁡(−αγN)+rNM\begin{document}$$\displaystyle r_{N}= (r_{N0}- r_{NM})\,\exp(-\alpha \gamma_{N}) + r_{NM} $$\end{document}(54)dN=dN0exp⁡(−αγN)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle d_{N}= d_{N0}\,\exp(-\alpha \gamma_{N}) $$\end{document}(55)sN=1−rN−dN\begin{document}$$\displaystyle s_{N}= 1 - r_{N} - d_{N} $$\end{document}

where rN0\begin{document}$r_{N0}$\end{document} and dN0\begin{document}$d_{N0}$\end{document} are the respective probabilities of repellency and induced mortality of a new ITN, while rNM\begin{document}$r_{NM}$\end{document} is the long-term probability of repellency from the physical barrier alone. Following a systematic review by Nash et al., 2021 that characterised the relationship between the level of resistance in wild mosquito populations, using the probability of bioassay survival as a proxy, and the probability of surviving 24 hr following exposure to a pyrethroid-only ITN (Sherrard-Smith et al., 2022) estimated the parameters in Equations 53–55 for a range of pyrethroid-resistance levels. This was conducted for both pyrethroid-only and pyrethroid-PBO ITNs from a suite of paired Experimental Hut Trials. This work has since been updated by Churcher et al., 2024 in the context of pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs and the models are broadly able to recreate the observed epidemiological benefit of different classes of ITNs evaluated in two cluster randomised control trials. Given estimated levels of pyrethroid resistance for each location over time, the probabilities of repellency and induced mortality for pyrethroid-only, pyrethroid-PBO, and pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr nets were parameterised for our transmission dynamics model accordingly.

sec.title: 5.4. Future case projections
sec.p: For each subnational region, 100 realisations were simulated for all ITN distribution strategies considered (biennial and triennial mass campaigns with pyrethroid-only, -PBO, and -chlorfenapyr ITNs) for a population of 100,000 individuals. We initialise all transmission models in January 2000 for each location, and assume continuous distribution over 2000–2007 at the same level as our historical estimates for January 2008. We then utilise our historical estimates of use from 2008 until our central estimates of the time of the last campaign, τL\begin{document}$\tau_{L}$\end{document}, before 2025. Given a mass campaign interval of Δτ\begin{document}$\Delta\tau$\end{document}, the timing of the first campaign of future projections, τF\begin{document}$\tau_{F}$\end{document}, is then drawn randomly from the interval τL+Δτ±6 months\begin{document}$\tau_{L}+\Delta\tau\pm 6\text{ months}$\end{document}. Subsequent mass campaigns occur after every Δτ\begin{document}$\Delta\tau$\end{document} interval thereafter. Pyrethroid-PBO ITNs are assumed to be distributed prior to 2025 through both continuous and mass campaign channels. All ITNs distributed from τF\begin{document}$\tau_{F}$\end{document} onwards are assumed to be of the new ITN type, again in both continuous and mass campaign contexts. Continued logistic growth in the number of ITNs distributed through continuous channels or in total use following a mass campaign is no longer assumed beyond 2024, modifying Equation 32 accordingly such that:(56)pij0(tj)={gi(January-2008), if tj<January-2008gi(December-2024), if tj>December-2024gi(tj), otherwise\begin{document}$$\displaystyle p_{ij}^{0}(t_{j}) = \begin{cases} g_{i}\left(\text{January-2008}\right)&\text{, if }t_{j} \lt \text{January-2008}\\ g_{i}\left(\text{December-2024}\right)&\text{, if }t_{j} \gt \text{December-2024}\\ g_{i}\left(t_{j}\right)&\text{, otherwise}\end{cases}$$\end{document}
wheregi(t)=ψilogit−1(βi0+βitt)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle g_{i}(t) = \psi_{i} \, \text{logit}^{-1}\left(\beta_{i}^{0}+\beta_{i}^{t} t \right)$$\end{document}

As ITN use is ultimately responsible for epidemiological impact, malariasimulation does not explicitly model access. For each realisation, values of qi0\begin{document}$q_{i}^{0}$\end{document}, λi\begin{document}$\lambda_{i}$\end{document}, ψi\begin{document}$\psi_{i}$\end{document}, βi0\begin{document}$\beta_{i}^{0}$\end{document}, and βit\begin{document}$\beta_{i}^{t}$\end{document} were therefore drawn from the joint posterior distribution from our discrete-time model of historical use (Equation 31), which was fitted using CmdStanR (v0.7.1, Gabry et al., 2024). Our estimates of the subnational variability in the probability of use and access (Equation 44) are captured in our posterior distributions of the overdispersion parameters, αi0\begin{document}$\alpha_{i}^{0}$\end{document}. Our discrete-time model cannot distinguish between spatial and temporal subregional variability. In practice, temporal heterogeneity is likely to be more significant for use than access due to seasonal fluctuations (e.g. use is likely to vary more between dry and wet seasons). To ensure compatibility with malariasimulation, for our transmission dynamics simulations we assume ITNs are used continuously before they cease to be used. Due to this incompatibility, subnational variability in the probability of use is therefore captured through stochastic binomial sampling in our transmission dynamics simulations rather than sampling from our posterior distribution for αi0\begin{document}$\alpha_{i}^{0}$\end{document}. The degree of over-reporting of use is simulated from Equation 52. Uncertainty in ITN repellency and mortality parameters (Equations 53 and 54) is also propagated forward to this study by simulating random draws from previous posterior distributions (Sherrard-Smith et al., 2022; Churcher et al., 2024) across each distribution event and realisation. Every 100 realisations for each scenario is simulated over 2000–2030 with the mean cases averted over the final 9 years recorded. We then restrict this to a period of 6 years following the first mass campaign under future projections to allow direct comparisons of cases averted between two triennial or three biennial campaigns; median time windows are used for future projections in the absence of mass campaigns. The maximum use estimated to be achieved by a campaign, had one been conducted at the end of 2024, is assumed to be maintained under future projections for each region. Similarly, the level of use of continuously distributed ITNs estimated at the end of 2024 for each region is assumed to be maintained. It is assumed that for a particular subnational region, the use achieved after a biennial campaign is the same as that under triennial campaigns. We generate estimates of clinical cases under different distribution strategies by simulating campaign intervals of 2 and 3 years, in addition to the cessation of mass campaigns entirely, over the 6-year projections. When switching from triennial to biennial campaigns, the model assumes those already with access are not excluded from mass campaigns, and accounts for diminishing returns in access as nets per capita increases (Bertozzi-Villa et al., 2021). It also assumes that use given access changes in the same manner to what was observed in triennial campaigns. All ITNs are assumed to be of the same type within a subnational region, and remain the same over subsequent mass campaigns. Routine distribution of ITNs, IRS, SMC and the level of drug treatment is assumed to continue as normal at the observed level. Posterior predictive estimates of cases averted are calculated from the additional cases averted over a baseline scenario where no future ITNs are distributed beyond our historical estimates (and those with nets lose them over time).

body.p: This work presents fundamental findings on the probability of use and access of inseticide-treated nets and evaluates the effectiveness of different distribution strategies in six African countries. The authors propose a sophisticated methodological framework that accounts for many sources of uncertainty, providing compelling strength of evidence.

[Editors' note: this version has been assessed by the Reviewing Editor without further input from the original reviewers. The authors have addressed the comments raised in the previous round of review.]

This paper aims to improve the accuracy of predictions of the impact of ITN strategies by developing a method to estimate duration of ITN access and use over time on a subnational scale from cross-sectional survey data and the numbers ITNs received annually. The subnational estimates are then input into a mathematical model to predict clinical cases under different ITN distribution strategies.
Strengths:
The approach is novel and addresses a useful and timely topic. It makes use of available routine data, and has considered all of the relevant components of ITN distributions.
The authors have made revisions, particularly to the methods, appendices and title - leaving the paper easier to follow, and with a clear, consistent aim. The assumptions are clearly stated.
Summary:

The authors design a custom Bayesian model to estimate the probabilities of access, use and use given access of insecticide-treated nets in six African countries, providing sub-national estimates and inferring the average duration of ITN use and access. An individual-based model was employed to simulate malaria epidemics and estimate the effectiveness of different ITN distribution strategies. The study finds that the mean probability of use or access did not reach 80% (a universal coverage formerly targeted by WHO) for any of the regions even for biennial campaigns, demonstrates that switching from triennial to biennial distribution campaigns increases population use by 7.9%, and evaluates the impact of employing more efficient ITNs on P. falciparum prevalence.
Strengths:

The authors developed a data-driven model that accounts for data collection imperfections and sources of uncertainty while differentiating between ITN use and access. They developed a methodology to infer the timing of mass campaign from publicly available data instead of assuming fixed dates. The probability of use given access allows determining the regions where ITN distribution is least effective. This work can help better inform future interventions by identifying regions where increasing mass campaign frequency or employing better ITNs are most effective. Finally, in addition to insights on ITN access and use for the six countries analyzed, the paper contributes with a methodological framework that can likely be extended to other countries.

disp-quote.p: P8 'Improving ITN use' L218

The numbers do not seem add up to me. "...increases across all settings of 14.5% (95% CrI:14.5, 14.6), from 41.7%% to 49.6%. Greater increases are predicted to be seen for ITN use with mean use across all settings increasing from 58.0% to 66.2%, an increase of 19.5% CrI (95% CrI:19.5, 19.6)."

body.p: Thank you for highlighting this. We have reviewed all reported results on mean use, access and use given access. The previous text reported a mixture of absolute and relative % changes, as well as a mixture of raw mean estimates across all regions and population-weighted means across regions. In the extract above we had inadvertently mixed different metrics. Given administrative-one regions can vary notably in population between different countries, we have ensured estimates are now consistently reported as population-weighted means, so that countries with finer-scaled administrative-one regions, such as Burkina Faso, do not artificially bias a raw mean estimate across all sub-national regions. We have also reported % changes as absolute percentage-point increases throughout, rather than relative ones to improve clarity.

disp-quote.p: Methods p18: There is notation in the text which does not seem to be explained. It is in the appendices, but the appendices should be optional extra information rather than essential for understanding.

body.p: We have reviewed the text in the main methods to check notation explanations. Following this, we have removed a use of subscript $i$, which is only used in the appendices to explicitly indicate region-specific parameters, and have clarified that lambda is a decay parameter.

disp-quote.p: There are assumptions made and these are clearly explained in the text. However, how much the highlighted results rest on the assumptions was not clear, and there was little on this in the discussion.

For example, it might seem disappointing that changing from triennial to biennial ITN campaigns would only lead to an increase from 41.7% to 49.6%. The most important assumptions driving this could be clearer. Additionally, after reading I was not sure what the likely consequences of the assumption that ITN are used continuously were.

body.p: We have added some additional text “to the discussion to clarify the modest predicted increase under biennial campaigns may, in part, be influenced by our assumed exponential loss function, and have highlighted that larger increases in mean use could plausibly be predicted under alternative ITN loss functions”. However, we have also commented that our mean use estimates are broadly in agreement with time series modelled estimates by Bertozzi-Villa et al. (2021) who utilised a sigmoidal/smooth-compact loss function.

In relation to the assumption of continuous use, we have added additional text in the ‘Historical use, access and retention times’ methods section to clarify that “if ITN use were systematically higher during high-transmission rainy seasons, our assumption of continuous use may underestimate the protective impact of ITNs during these periods”. As stated at the start of that paragraph, the data available from DHS surveys was too infrequent to investigate seasonal fluctuations.

disp-quote.p: P14 The text seems to imply that current transmission intensity is the only criterion for decisions about interventions. However, it is likely that the reasons for the current intensity, such as vectorial capacity, historical transmission and interventions should also play a role. The wording could reflect this.

body.p: We have added additional text to clarify that current transmission intensity should not be treated as the only criterion for deprioritisation decisions:

“However, current incidence should be considered alongside the factors that gave rise to that transmission intensity, with caution exercised when deprioritising mass campaigns in areas where historically higher transmission may currently be suppressed by high ITN access, high use given access, or other interventions.”

disp-quote.p: Minor points
There are several definite numbers in the first paragraph of the Introduction - these are estimates rather than the absolute truth, but the wording does not acknowledge that there is uncertainty.

body.p: We have made minor edits to clarify that these values are estimates rather than exact quantities. Measures of uncertainty, such as credible intervals were not always possible to source; for example, some of these are median estimates inferred from figures in Bertozzi-Villa et al. (2021).
